title: How to Build a Retirement Plan for a Single-Income Household
description: Securing the future for stay-at-home spouses and single earners.
content:
Retirement planning is often discussed in terms of 'dual income power.' But for millions of households—either single parents, singles, or couples with a stay-at-home spouse—the reality is one income stream funding the future of one (or two) people. This creates a 'concentration risk.' If the earner can't work, the plan fails. Single-income households need a 'Fortress' strategy: higher savings rates, robust insurance, and specific legal protections like the Spousal IRA.

Key Takeaways

  • The Spousal IRA: A non-working spouse can have an IRA funded by the working spouse's income. This doubles the IRA space ($14,000 total). Use it.
  • Life Insurance Multiplier: If a stay-at-home spouse dies, childcare costs skyrocket. If the earner dies, income stops. You need massive Term Life policies on *both* partners.
  • Social Security Spousal Benefit: The non-working spouse is entitled to 50% of the worker's benefit at FRA. This means the household gets 1.5x the check, not 1x. Factor this into your gap analysis.
  • Higher Savings Rate: One income means less room for error. Aim to save 25% of gross income to build a buffer against layoffs.

Why It Matters (US Context)

The tax code favors single-income married couples (Joint Filing) up to certain limits. Leveraging the standard deduction ($29,200) against one income creates tax efficiency that can be redirected to savings.

The Single-Income Math

Scenario: Married, One Earner ($100k).

The Vulnerability

If Earner gets sick, savings stop and spending continues.
Defense: You need Own Occupation Disability Insurance. It replaces the paycheck.

The Savings Stack

  • 401(k): Earner puts in $23,000.
  • Roth IRA (Earner): $7,000.
  • Roth IRA (Spouse): $7,000.
  • Total Capacity: $37,000 (37% savings rate).

The Social Security Boost

Earner Benefit: $3,000/mo.
Spousal Benefit: $1,500/mo.
Total Household: $4,500/mo ($54k/year).
This guaranteed floor reduces the portfolio need significantly.

Tactical Steps

  1. Widow Planning: If the earner dies, the household loses one SS check (the smaller one) but keeps the larger one. Ensure the survivor has enough assets to cover the income drop.
  2. The 'Stay-at-Home' Career: Even if not earning, the non-working spouse should keep skills fresh. If the earner is laid off, the ability for the spouse to 'tag in' and get a job is the ultimate emergency fund.
  3. Aggressive Debt Payoff: Enter retirement with a paid-off house. A single income cannot service a mortgage in retirement safely.
  4. Legal Hygiene: Ensure both names are on all accounts. In a crisis, you don't want assets frozen because the account holder is incapacitated.

Frequently Asked Questions

Can a non-working spouse open a Roth?

Yes, 'Spousal Roth IRA'. The working spouse must have enough earned income to cover both contributions. It is a powerful tool.

What about divorce?

Retirement accounts accumulated during marriage are generally split 50/50. The non-earner is protected legally, but having separate credit history is smart.

Is it harder to retire?

Yes. You have one engine pulling the weight of two people. Discipline is higher. You can't rely on 'two incomes' to mask spending problems.
